status: A bounded factual and assessment clarification of the existing social-hierarchy claim, separate from any new curriculum association or learner-state decision.

before.description: Describe the social structure of ancient Egypt as a pyramid-shaped hierarchy: the pharaoh at the top, then priests and nobles, followed by scribes and soldiers, then craftworkers and merchants, and farmers and labourers at the base — understanding that a person's position was usually inherited and determined their whole way of life
evidence: Draw or describe the social pyramid with at least four levels correctly ordered
Explain that most people were farmers and had very different lives from the pharaoh
Give an example of how social position affected someone's daily life (e.g., only scribes could read)
before.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked who was more important in ancient Egypt — a scribe or a farmer — can they explain the social pyramid and where each person fitted?

after.description: Describe a simplified model of ancient Egyptian social hierarchy: the pharaoh at the top, then priests and nobles, followed by scribes and soldiers, then craftworkers and merchants, with farmers and labourers at the base. Family background and status often shaped people’s work, resources and opportunities, while some people could move to a different position.
evidence: Draw or describe the social pyramid with at least four levels correctly ordered
Explain that most people were farmers and had very different lives from the pharaoh

Give a supported example of how social position affected daily work or access to resources, such as scribes keeping administrative records while farmers grew crops; do not assume that only professional scribes could read.
after.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe the studied Egyptian social hierarchy, placing at least four groups in the model, and explain how rank, power and work differed—for example, between a scribe and a farmer? Higher rank does not mean greater human worth, and social position was not an unchangeable rule for every person.

rationale: Professional scribes were not the only people able to read. Literacy varied, and surviving evidence includes literate priests, officials and some other workers. The corrected example tests supported work/status differences without an exclusive literacy rule.
Family background and social position could shape opportunities without determining every detail of every life or making movement impossible. The simplified hierarchy remains a model.
Social rank and power are not a judgment of human worth. The prompt now elicits the same ordered-group and daily-work understanding directly.
